```{r, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

Of course, it is possible to generate tibbles manually. We just need to copy and paste the data from the resource into the R script. This approach works fine if we have a couple of data points (referred to as observations). However, it gets cumbersome if we need to work with something closer to real-world problems in R. In the following section, we will focus on how to get the data into R (so-called data import) and a little bit on how to produce the data from R (data export). In terms of the data science pipeline, the whole data science project starts with **data import**.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("illustrations/fig-data-import.png")
```

# Delimited files

::: blackbox
**Disclaimer:** Some data used in this section are simulated and have nothing to do with real-world figures.
:::

<br>

The idea of delimited files is straightforward: they separate the data entries with a specific delimiter character, such as a comma (`,`), for instance, or character tabulation (tab for short). These delimited characters give names for the two most wide-spreader file types, namely CSV (comma-separated values) and TSV (tab-separated values):

```{r, echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("illustrations/1-delim.png")
```

## `read_csv()`

A file on your machine called `team.csv` is in the folder `data`. We encourage you to inspect this file by opening it in TextEdit (if you use macOS) or Notepad (if you use Windows). Luckily, R has dozens of functions that allow importing such files (in R jargon, importing files is called reading). We will consider functions from the `{readr}` package, which is a part of `{tidyverse}`. These functions are fast, reliable, and have a very consistent syntax. Each function name starts with the verb `read` followed by the underscore `_` and is finally appended with the delimiter type. For example, the function `read_csv()` will read CSV files.

We need to provide the path to the file. In our case, this is `"data/team.csv"` (please do not worry for now if you are concerned that we provide a short version of the path). Since we want to capture the data into an object (in other words, assign it to the object), your pattern would be similar to what follows next:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
name_of_object <- read_csv("path_to_file")
```

Let's try to apply this pattern to the `team.csv` file. Since the function `read_csv()` comes from the `{readr}` package, we need to load it first. The code would look like that:

```{r, eval=TRUE}
library(readr)

team <- read_csv("data/team.csv")
```

Let's see what our data look like:

```{r}
team
```

### Absolute vs relative paths

You may have noticed that we used quite short paths for the file that did not include your personal folder structure. This is extremely beneficial because if you'd like to share your code with your collaborator, they do not have to change any paths. For example, rather than having `"/Users/jack/Documents/your/unique/folder/structure/data/team.csv"`, we can refer to this file as `"data/team.csv"`. This feature works only with R Markdown files or if you have created an RStudio project.

### Column names

By default, `read_csv()` uses the first row of the file as column names (e.g., `name`, `gender`, and so on, in the example above). Sometimes, however, the file's first row is data itself rather than the column names. A dedicated argument, `col_names`, defines how to treat the first row. If the first row does not contain names, it should be set to `FALSE`.

The content of the file `team_wo_header.csv` on your computer looks as follows:

```{r, comment=NA, echo=FALSE}
team_wo_header_csv <- read_lines(file = "data/team_wo_header.csv")
team_wo_header_csv[1:4] %>% str_c(collapse = "\n") %>% cat()
```

You see that it does not have a header (i.e., column names). Let's read this file and set `col_names` to `FALSE`:

```{r}
team_wo_header <- read_csv("data/team_wo_header.csv", col_names = FALSE)

team_wo_header
```

R auto-generates column names: `X1`, `X2`, etc.

### Missing values

Sometimes, when CSV files are generated by other software, the missing values can be decoded differently from what R would expect. For example, if missing values are denoted by the `"null"` string, R won't recognize them as missing values but rather consider them as ordinary strings of characters `"null"`. Let's have a look:

```{r, comment=NA, echo=FALSE}
team_missing_csv <- read_lines(file = "data/team_missing.csv")
team_missing_csv[1:4] %>% str_c(collapse = "\n") %>% cat()
```

Applying `read_csv()` as is would lead to wrong column types (we will come back to data types in the data wrangling part) and wrong interpretation of `"null"`:

```{r}
team_missing <- read_csv("data/team_missing.csv")
team_missing
```

Fear not, `read_csv()` has an argument `na` to specify strings that would be interpreted as missing values. Setting `na` to `"null"` would solve this issue:

```{r}
team_missing <- read_csv("data/team_missing.csv", na = "null")
team_missing
```

### `skip`

The CSV files do not always have the extension `.csv`, and sometimes they are saved as `.txt` files. This is not a problem for `read_csv()`. In addition, these files might have the data description in the first lines (so-called meta-data or data about data). When importing the data into tibble, these lines of meta-data should be skipped, and the name of the argument that controls how many rows to skip is called, surprise, `skip`. Therefore, to read this file

```{r, comment=NA, echo=FALSE}
team_missing_csv <- read_lines(file = "data/team_meta.txt")
team_missing_csv[1:7] %>% str_c(collapse = "\n") %>% cat()
```

we will need to skip three first rows

```{r}
team_meta <- read_csv("data/team_meta.txt", skip = 3)
team_meta
```

### Other arguments

There are other useful arguments that allow controlling the importing process. As a reminder, you can always read the help of the function by `?read_csv`. One such argument is `locale`. Suppose you have a CSV file with special letters from French or German (or any other language). In that case, you can set `locale` to `locale(encoding = "latin1")` to enable `latin1` encoding (most European languages have full coverage). Compare the output of the following code chunks:

```{r}
cities <- read_csv("data/cities.csv")
cities
```

```{r}
cities <- read_csv("data/cities.csv", locale = locale(encoding = "latin1"))
cities
```

The nice thing about `{readr}` is that all the above-mentioned arguments are available in other functions that we will consider further, namely `read_csv2()`, `read_tsv()`, and `read_delim()`.

**Trick:** After you have typed the name of the function and both parentheses, you can move your cursor inside the parentheses and press <kbd>Tab</kbd>. The function's argument list will pop up, and you can select the one you need and even read a short description.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("illustrations/1-read_csv.png")
```

## `read_csv()` siblings: `read_csv2()`, `read_tsv()`, `read_delim()`

Since the function `read_csv()` uses a comma (`,`) as a delimiter, the decimal mark is automatically assumed to be a dot `.`. Otherwise, there is no way to distinguish which comma separates data entries and which one signifies the decimal point. In countries that use commas as decimal points, the delimiter is typically a semicolon (`;`). There is a twin sibling of `read_csv()` -- `read_csv2()`, which is designed to read files with the `;` delimiter and the `,` decimal point.

There are two other members of the family, namely `read_tsv()` and `read_delim()`. The former assumes a tabular as a delimiter, while you can specify the delimiter by yourself in `read_delim()`.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The `{readr}` functions that read delimiter files are summarized in the table below. Typically, you will mostly use the first three functions.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
tribble(
  ~ `Function`, ~ `Delimiter`, ~ `Default decimal`,
  "`read_csv()`", "`,` (comma)", "`.` (dot)",
  "`read_csv2()`", "`;` (semicolon)", "`,` (comma)",
  "`read_tsv()`", "Tab", "`.` (dot)",
  "`read_delim()`", "Custom", "`.` (dot)",
) %>%
  kable()
```

As a final word, CSV files are the most common file format for sharing small- and mid-sized data (up to several Gb). The main advantage is that CSV files are software-agnostic. That means it should be possible to read such files regardless of the software you use. It is especially important if you work in a team that uses several different tools and programming languages.

# Excel files

Chances that you have never been asked to work with Excel sheets tend to zero. Perhaps, it could be the most popular format for storing small datasets. In this section, we will learn how to import data from Excel files, both legacy `.xls` and current `.xlsx` formats.

## `{readxl}`

There are plenty of packages in R that can read the data from Excel. We will focus on `{readxl}` package which is a part of `{tidyverse}`. Even though `{readxl}` is a part of `{tidyverse}`, it is not included into its core part. Therefore, we will need to install it separately:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("readxl")
```

Once it is installed, we can load it:

```{r}
library(readxl)
```

To read the data from Excel into R, we use several function, namely `read_xls()` and `read_xlsx()` for `.xls` and `.xlsx` file formats, respectively. There is also `read_excel()` that can guess the file format automatically. Naturally, the first argument of the function is the file path, just like in `read_csv()`.

The `team` dataset is also saved as an Excel file, and to read it, we will use `read_xlsx()`. Before jumping to the next line, please open the file and have a look at how it is structured.

```{r}
team <- read_xlsx("data/team.xlsx")
team
```

Works like a charm! But Excel files are not always that clean and tidy. For instance, the file `je-e-06.02.00.01.02.xlsx` in the folder `data` does not look very clean. At the end of this section, you should be able to get any data that you need from this Excel file. But first, let's scroll over the useful arguments:

### `sheet`

The Excel file can have multiple sheets and the argument `sheet` controls which sheet should be read into tibble. It can be passed as a character representation of the sheet (e.g., `"Seasonally adjusted total"`) or as the numerical index (e.g., `2`). By default, `read_xlsx()` uses the first sheet, and we can easily alternate that:

```{r}
women_jobs <- read_xlsx(
  "data/je-e-06.02.00.01.02.xlsx",
  sheet = "Women"
)

women_jobs
```

There is definitely something that went wrong, so it is not enough to provide only the sheet.

### `range`

The reason why specifying the `sheet` is not enough is that we have data all over the place, and it is not easy where the data is located. We can refer to a rectangular cell range by specifying its upper left and lower right cell separated by `:`, for example, `B2:K14`. This notion is implemented as the `range` argument of `read_xlsx()` and friends -- we can specify a particular range that will be treated as data.

We can modify our initial expression to accommodate a particular range, say between A9 and DP72:

```{r}
women_jobs <- read_xlsx(
  "data/je-e-06.02.00.01.02.xlsx",
  sheet = "Women",
  range = "A9:DP72"
)

women_jobs
```

We are one step closer, but still not there. The column names contain values, so we need somehow to let R know that we need to treat them as values instead. But that's something that we've learned already, right?

### `col_names`

Well, yes. The function `read_xlsx()` has an identical argument `col_names` as the function `read_csv()`. The behavior is absolutely the same, and you know what to expect -- set it to `FALSE`, and the first line won't be considered as column names.

```{r}
women_jobs <- read_xlsx(
  "data/je-e-06.02.00.01.02.xlsx",
  sheet = "Women",
  range = "A9:DP72", 
  col_names = FALSE, 
)

women_jobs
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("illustrations/2-excel.png")
```

# Files generated by statistical software

The data also might come in the file format that was generated with statistical software, such as SAS, SPSS, or Stata. These tools used to be (for some cases, even still is) extremely popular among government institutions, pharmaceutical companies, and research labs. As is, R cannot read legacy files produces by listed programs. However, there is a nice package called `{haven}` that allows reading and writing `.sas7bdat`, `.sas7bcat`, `.sav`, `.por`, `.dta`, and other extensions.

Below, we provide a summary table of which function to use:

```{r, echo=FALSE}
tribble(
  ~ `File extenssion`, ~ `Software`, ~ `Function`,
  "`.sas7bdat`", "SAS", "`read_sas()`",
  "`.sas7bcat`", "SAS", "`read_sas()`",
  "`.xpt`", "SAS", "`read_xpt()`",
  "`.sav`", "SPSS", "`read_sav()`",
  "`.por`", "SPSS", "`read_por()`",
  "`.dta`", "Stata", "`read_dta()`"
) %>%
  kable()
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("illustrations/3-other.png")
```

For instance, let's see how to import the files of SAS data output with `read_sas()`.

```{r}
library(haven)

mtcars_data <- read_sas("data/mtcars.sas7bdat")
```

Let's print this import to see whether the data has been imported properly:

```{r}
mtcars_data
```

Everything looks A-OK!

Since these file types are very specific, we won't cover each and every argument. The nice thing about `{tidyverse}` is that it is well documented, and in case if you need a particular feature, you can always read the documentation.
